catalog_quote: Kasiguranin word stress or accent is normally predictable on the terminal syllable of a word and uses high pitch level on the terminal syllables of the words, which makes it different from Filipino language which uses low pitch level on the terminal syllables, as shown by a number of minimal pairs, such as: KL /abusado (3)/ FL /abusado (1)/ ... /bota (3)/ /bota (1)/ Kasiguranin words containing closed penultimate syllables are variably accented on the ultimate or the penultima, without any corresponding change in meaning: /abusadó/-/abusádo/ “abusive”; /buhayá/-/buwáya/ “alligator”; /dambaná/-/dambána/ “altar”; /rayumá/-/rayúma/ “arthritis”; /botá/-/bóta/ “boots.” The basic phonological difference between Kasiguranin Language and Filipino Language chiefly concern intonation contours, having a melodic glide within the syllables, especially in the word-terminal syllables. new_statements.rule_in_words: Per this source, word accent normally falls on the final syllable, realised as high pitch on that syllable; a set of (loan) words varies freely between final and penultimate accent with no meaning difference. Caveats: the author is not a linguist, the 'closed penultimate syllables' condition does not fit his own examples (all open penults), and the only modern linguists' data (Robinson & Lobel 2013) transcribe Kasiguranin forms with per-word accent, mostly final (57/64) but some penult (dígus, dúwa, ágtaʔ, apérit), which for a Tagalog-descended language with Agta loans points rather to lexically contrastive accent with a final-syllable majority. Treat the fixed: final syllable reading as provisional pending Supnet 2016.
new_statements.exceptions: Free variation ultima ~ penult 'without any corresponding change in meaning' in abusado, buhaya/buwaya, dambana, rayuma, bota (all Spanish/Tagalog-shared items).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level citation forms elicited from Casiguran, Aurora residents; statement framed contrastively against Filipino/Tagalog pitch levels; intonation contours discussed separately (yes-no questions use fall/sustention rather than Tagalog rise).
new_statements.identity_note: Both accessible sources describe the speech of the non-Agta town-centre population of Casiguran, Aurora (Kasiguranin, kasi1256/ksn), not Casiguran Dumagat Agta (casi1235/dgc), which is a different (Northeastern Luzon) language with its own accent description (Headland & Healey 1974). Robinson & Lobel 2013 treat Kasiguranin as a Tagalog descendant outside the NELUZ subgroup, so their Table 11 'loss of contrastive stress' for NE Luzon does not apply to it.

sources.note: Sec. 4.2.1 'Phonological aspect', p. 231: word stress/accent 'normally predictable on the terminal syllable of a word', realised with high pitch on the final syllable (contrasted with Filipino/Tagalog); some words 'variably accented on the ultimate or the penultima, without any corresponding change in meaning' (abusadó ~ abusádo, buhayá ~ buwáya, dambaná ~ dambána, rayumá ~ rayúma, botá ~ bóta). Author is an education-faculty lexicographer (NEUST); fieldwork with 122 native residents of Casiguran, Aurora; cites his unpublished 2015 NEUST MA thesis.

sources.note: No explicit statement about Kasiguranin stress. Kasiguranin (KAS) forms are cited with acute accent marks throughout sec. 2.1; of 64 accent-marked KAS forms, 57 have the accent on the final syllable and 7 on the penult (dígus 'bathe', dúwa 'two', ágtaʔ, apérit 'short', adɛ́ne 'near', kɛ́nam, tóglad), i.e. accent position is recorded per word. Table 11 (p. 156) row 9 'Loss of contrastive stress: NE Luzon YES' refers to the NELUZ languages, from which Kasiguranin is explicitly excluded (sec. 1.2, pp. 129-130: descendant of an early Tagalog dialect).
